extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students in psychology/cognitive science of humor; academics studying emotion and humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Presentation and experimental test of the Play‑Mirth cognitive appraisal theory of humor, specifying appraisals that elicit mirth and how to measure them. Includes definitions, hypotheses, operational measures, and experimental findings differentiating humorous from nonhumorous experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful turn (core appraisal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rapid and instantaneous cognitive shift from something viewed as (more) serious to something now seen as less serious (or more playful). It is the reinterpretation of a (relatively) serious identity (person/object/situation/statement/conversation) in a less serious/playful way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be rapid to heighten contrast; can be intentional or unintentional; can take many forms (metaphor, hyperbole, irony, sarcasm, overstatement, understatement, incongruity resolution, simple juxtaposition). Can be people-oriented (disparagement, teasing) or non-people-oriented (food humor, wordplay, scatological), meaningful (semantically relevant opposites) or nonsense/absurd (semantically irrelevant juxtaposition). Playful turn intensity predicts humor intensity; novelty increases reward prediction error and thus increases humor, but stock (repeated) turns can still trigger humor until habituation. Examples: ironic compliment reframing a serious candidacy as unserious; forgetting to zip is an unintentional playful turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive-consistency (core appraisal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The appraisal that the playful turn is consistent with an individual's motives — i.e., it is 'good for us' or aligned with what the individual wants, improving things for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motive-consistency is necessary (with playful turn) for mirth. It can satisfy one or multiple motives (enjoyment, relief, superiority, etc.). A playful turn consistent with some motives but inconsistent with others elicits less humor (mixed emotions). A joke that is inconsistent with the individual's wants is unlikely to be humorous. This concept contrasts with 'benign' in benign-violation theory: motive-consistency is about goodness for the individual's wants, not general 'no harm'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunctive requirement for humor (Play‑Mirth hypothesis / H1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor (mirth) occurs if and only if two appraisals occur simultaneously: (a) perception of a playful turn, and (b) the playful turn is considered consistent with the individual's motive(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central empirical claim tested in the paper: both conditions must be satisfied to elicit mirth. The authors operationalize and test this conjunction in experiments and find supportive evidence (playful turn and motive-consistency strongly distinguish successful from failed jokes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness (appraisal / enhancer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the stimulus (playful turn) is unexpected or novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpectedness has a positive effect on mirth (hypothesized H2) by increasing reward prediction error and dopamine response, but it is neither necessary nor sufficient for humor. Unexpectedness enhances but does not alone guarantee humor. Measured with adapted Roseman et al. items (e.g., expected/unexpected).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance (appraisal / enhancer)
rubrics_metrics.description: How relevant the playful turn is to the prior conversation or situational context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevance positively affects mirth (hypothesized H3) and can increase humor appreciation; however, relevance is not strictly necessary nor sufficient by itself. Measured by items such as 'was relevant to the prior conversation.' In experiments relevance differed less strongly than playful turn and motive-consistency between successful and failed jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivational state: appetitive vs aversive (reward vs relief humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between appetitive (reward-seeking) and aversive (pain-avoiding) motivational states that modulate the type of humor experienced—reward-humor vs relief-humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both appetitive and aversive motives can elicit mirth if the playful turn is motive-consistent; the motivational state differentiates the flavor/type of mirth (joy-like reward vs relief-like). Measured via motivational-state items adapted from Roseman (e.g., wanting to get/keep something pleasurable vs wanting to avoid something painful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty vs stock playful turns (repetition & habituation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the playful turn is novel/unexpected or a previously used ('stock') turn that is relevant to prior exposures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel playful turns produce a larger reward prediction error and stronger dopamine responses; stock turns rely on stimulus recall and yield reduced but immediate responses. Humor wears out with repetition; novelty increases mirth but is not strictly necessary if relevance/association remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign violation (comparison metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: From benign-violation theory: humor occurs when an event is appraised both as a violation and as benign (not threatening).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper treats benign violation as an important prior criterion but contrasts it with motive-consistency: benign = 'makes us feel okay' vs motive-consistency = 'good for our wants'. Benign violations may elicit mixed emotions and do not fully account for absurd or nonsense humor. Measured in the study with a 2-item scale (e.g., seen as both wrong and not wrong).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminishment / reversal theory constructs (comparison metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal theory's idea that humor involves cognitive synergy and diminishment (a change in interpretation that reduces an identity's value) and typically requires a playful motivational state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguished from playful turn: diminishment is broader (many diminishments are not playful turns) and reversal theory often requires the observer to already be in a playful state; Play‑Mirth allows playful turns to occur even when observers are in serious states (humor can cause the switch). Use as a comparative framework rather than a replacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms/modalities of playful turn (qualifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The possible linguistic/behavioral forms that implement a playful turn: metaphor, hyperbole, irony, sarcasm, overstatement, understatement, incongruity resolution, juxtaposition, malapropism, wordplay, nonsense/absurd juxtapositions, bodily/physical comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are mechanisms through which playful turns are instantiated. They influence perceived sophistication, social acceptability, and whether the turn is people- or non-people-oriented; they can determine relevance and motive-consistency in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: People-oriented vs non-people-oriented playful turns
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the playful turn targets persons (disparagement, teasing, sexist jokes) or non-personal objects/topics (food humor, witty wordplay, scatology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People-oriented turns interact with social motives (e.g., bonding, superiority) and can produce mixed motives (e.g., enjoyment vs harm to relationship). Motive-consistency must be considered across social goals: a joke that is humorous for one motive may violate another motive (reducing humor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational measurement scales (experimental metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of questionnaire/scales used to assess appraisals and emotional responses in experiments: playful turn (5-item scale), motive-consistency (5 items), unexpectedness (3 items), motivational state (4 items), relevance (2 items), benign violation (2 items), mirth (3 items: 'It was funny/amusing/humorous'), plus single items for joy, relief, laughter, negative emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All items measured on 9-point Likert scales; instrument reliabilities reported (Cronbach's alpha values). The paper uses these operational measures to distinguish successful from failed jokes and to test hypotheses. Researchers should use validated items (adapted from Roseman et al. and related sources) and account for multiple comparisons (e.g., Bonferroni adjustments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mirth as the target emotion (distinct from joy/relief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mirth defined as a short-lived positive emotion elicited by the conjunction of playful turn and motive-consistency; operationalized by items capturing perceived funniness/amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play‑Mirth theory argues mirth is distinct from other positive emotions like joy and relief and has its own appraisal pattern (playful turn + motive-consistency). Empirically measure and distinguish mirth from related emotions using separate items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictors of successful vs failed humor (empirical discriminators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical finding: successful jokes show higher levels of playful turn intensity and motive-consistency (largest differences), as well as higher unexpectedness and benign violation, compared to failed jokes; relevance differentiates less strongly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use playful turn and motive-consistency as primary discriminators when evaluating why humor succeeded or failed. Consider effect sizes and correct for multiple testing. Failed humor often corresponds to low motive-consistency even if playful turn is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of humor (non-tautological)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor defined as the rapid and instantaneous perception of life as less serious and more playful that elicits the positive short-lived emotion of mirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition focuses on the cognitive appraisal (shift from seriousness to playfulness) and emotional outcome (mirth), avoiding tautological formulations. Use this definition to distinguish humor from general play and from other emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed-motive and appropriateness constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: A playful turn that is consistent with some motives but inconsistent with others yields reduced humor and possibly mixed emotions; motive-consistency is also an appropriateness gauge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing humor's social acceptability or likely success in context (e.g., leader humor, interpersonal settings), evaluate multiple relevant motives (bonding, superiority, relief, enjoyment) because conflict among them predicts reduced mirth or social costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habituation and wear-out as a quality constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated exposure to the same playful turn reduces the reward prediction error and the perceived funniness over time (humor wears out with repetition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider novelty and timing when designing or evaluating humorous material; stock turns may function but will decline in effectiveness with repeated use.
